metadata.title: Teacher vs. Machine Correction: Comparing Assessments of Students’ Reading Comprehension and Written Summaries
metadata.venue: Journal of Research in Applied Linguistics, 15(2)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses a small, purpose-built sample of 30 Spanish students (aged 14–16) and 30 teachers who corrected photocopied summaries, rather than an international large-scale assessment sampling frame. Although the reading text is taken from PISA 2009, the analysis is based on teacher–machine scoring comparisons and latent class/correspondence analysis, not on population-representative estimation. The manuscript does not report the use of PISA student sampling weights or any complex survey design weights (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) for inference; therefore, results should be interpreted as evidence about scoring similarity within this experimental setup. No PV scaling or achievement-score weighting is involved because the dependent construct is teacher–system dissimilarity derived from rubric-style scores.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the study does not model PISA cognitive achievement PV-based outcomes; instead, it compares teacher and G-Rubric scores on a single PISA 2009 text-summary task and derives Euclidean-distance dissimilarity categories. Missing-data handling is not reported because the paper describes exclusions related to informed consent and achieving a homogeneous teacher sample, but it does not specify a missingness rule for item-level or score-level missing data within the analytic dataset. As a result, the transparency needed to assess potential bias from missingness is limited.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Students: 30 Spanish students aged 14–16 (16 females, 14 males) recruited at five Spanish secondary school centers selected randomly; they completed a PISA 2009 reading comprehension text-summary task (385-word text) and produced summaries of 60–100 words. Teachers: 30 Spanish language instructors from five regions (Madrid, Castilla la Mancha, Andalucía, Extremadura, Asturias) were selected at random to correct the 30 summaries; from 51 submitted corrections, 21 were disapproved (5 for failure to provide informed consent; 16 to ensure a homogeneous sample reflecting sex, age, and teaching-experience study variables). Teachers were not informed that their scores would be compared to other teachers or to G-Rubric; they scored on paper using their normal criteria, and then age/sex/experience were computed for analysis.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009 reading comprehension text-summary task the study leveraged Teacher sex, Teacher age group, Teaching experience group to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This study experimentally compares human teacher scoring with the automatic correction system G-Rubric on a Spanish reading comprehension task drawn from PISA 2009. Thirty Spanish students (aged 14–16) wrote 60–100 word summaries of a 385-word text; 30 teachers then scored the summaries on style and content, while G-Rubric produced corresponding rubric-based scores. The analysis uses Euclidean distance between each teacher’s 30 style and 30 content scores and the system’s scores, categorizing dissimilarity into low/medium/high via quartiles, and then applying latent class analysis (Latent Gold 4.5) and correspondence analysis (SPSS) to identify teacher profiles. The best-fitting latent class solution is a three-cluster model (lowest BIC among 1–4 clusters), with dissimilarity explained at R²=0.5729 and cluster membership associated with teacher age and experience (sex not significant at conventional levels). The study reports cluster sizes of 41.26% (Cluster 1), 34.48% (Cluster 2, lowest dissimilarity), and 24.26% (Cluster 3, highest dissimilarity), and concludes that scoring similarity varies by teacher demographics, suggesting G-Rubric may be more aligned with certain teacher profiles. Limitations include the small, non-representative sample and the absence of PV-based achievement modeling or survey-weighted inference. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper is an experimental scoring-comparison study that uses latent class analysis and correspondence analysis to typologize teacher–machine dissimilarity; it does not train or evaluate machine-learning predictive models. Consequently, the schema’s ML technique fields are left empty, and main_findings are not populated because the study’s outcomes are clustering/profile results rather than predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE) for a supervised target.
